mean: to shoulder the key role or main responsibility
lit: to carry the main roof beam on one's shoulders

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often split as 挑起大梁 or 挑起了…的大梁. Said of a person or group taking the central role in a team, project or performance.

near.diff: 一把手 is the person in the top post; 挑大梁 is whoever actually carries the main load, whatever their title.
跑龙套 is the opposite: having only a small part that anyone could fill.

cue: The star striker is injured, and a nineteen-year-old suddenly becomes the player the whole team relies on to win. What has he done?

ctx.s: 老师傅退休了，现在由小王{挑大梁}。
ctx.en: The old master has retired, and now Xiao Wang carries the main load.

ctx.s: 这次项目是你第一次{挑大梁}，紧张吗？
ctx.en: This project is the first time you've taken the lead role. Nervous?

ctx.s: 主力队员受伤以后，这个十九岁的新人{挑起了大梁}。
ctx.en: After the key players were injured, this nineteen-year-old newcomer took on the team's main burden.

ctx.s: 公司现在缺的不是普通员工，而是能{挑大梁}的人。
ctx.en: What the company lacks now is not ordinary staff but people who can shoulder the key responsibilities.

ctx.s: “这部戏谁演主角？”“这回让年轻演员{挑大梁}。”
ctx.en: "Who's playing the lead in this play?" "This time we're letting a young actor carry the show."

ctx.s: 经过几年锻炼，这批年轻人已经能在单位里{挑起大梁}了。
ctx.en: After a few years of experience, this group of young people can now shoulder the main work of the organisation.

bad.s: 搬家那天，他一个人{挑大梁}，把冰箱扛上了五楼。
bad.en: (meant: on moving day he carried the fridge up to the fifth floor by himself)
bad.why: It is figurative: taking the central role in work, a team or a show, not physically carrying something heavy.

bad.s: 他{挑大梁}了这个项目。
bad.en: (meant: he took the lead on this project)
bad.why: It is already verb plus object and takes no further object; say zai zhege xiangmu li tiao daliang (take the lead in this project).

mean: to play only a minor, supporting part
lit: to run about the stage in the dragon-patterned extras' costume

story.text: In traditional Chinese opera, the extras who play soldiers, guards and attendants wear a standard costume embroidered with dragons, called a longtao. They come on in a group, run across the stage, stand in formation around the main characters and run off again, usually without lines of their own. Running in the longtao came to mean having only a small part in anything.
story.source: Stage term of traditional Chinese opera (京剧 and other 戏曲)

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often as 跑龙套的 (an extra) or split as 跑了几年龙套. Said of oneself or others having only a minor role, often modestly or wryly.

near.diff: 挑大梁 is carrying the main role; 跑龙套 is the opposite, a small supporting part.

cue: Asked about his part in an award-winning project, a junior designer shrugs and says he only fetched files and booked meeting rooms. How does he describe his role?

ctx.s: 我在这部电影里只是{跑龙套}的，镜头不到一分钟。
ctx.en: I'm only an extra in this film; I'm on screen for less than a minute.

ctx.s: 他在剧组{跑了五年龙套}，才演上第一个有台词的角色。
ctx.en: He played bit parts for five years before he got his first role with lines.

ctx.s: “这次活动你负责什么？”“我就是{跑跑龙套}，帮忙搬搬东西。”
ctx.en: "What are you in charge of at this event?" "I'm just helping out on the side, carrying things around."

ctx.s: 别看他现在是大明星，当年也是从{跑龙套}开始的。
ctx.en: He may be a big star now, but he started out as an extra.

ctx.s: 这个项目我们部门只是{跑龙套}，主要工作都是总部做的。
ctx.en: Our department only played a supporting part in this project; headquarters did the main work.

ctx.s: 他不甘心一辈子在公司里{跑龙套}，决定出去自己创业。
ctx.en: Unwilling to spend his whole career in minor roles at the company, he decided to leave and start his own business.

bad.s: 他是我们公司的总经理，每天都在{跑龙套}。
bad.en: (meant: he is our general manager and rushes about busily every day)
bad.why: It does not mean rushing about busily; it means having a minor, unimportant part, so it cannot describe the boss's busy day.

bad.s: 我想{跑龙套}这个角色。
bad.en: (meant: I want to play this small role)
bad.why: It is already verb plus object and takes no further object; say zai zhe bu xi li pao longtao (play a bit part in this show).

mean: to give someone special extra attention or coaching
lit: to fire up a small stove: cook a separate, better meal apart from the big communal kitchen

use.how: Verb-object phrase, usually 给某人开小灶 or 开个小灶. Said of extra one-to-one help or special treatment from a teacher, coach or boss; can hint at favouritism.

near.diff: 走后门 is getting an advantage through connections, usually improperly; 开小灶 is someone in charge giving one person extra help or better treatment.

cue: A student keeps failing maths, so her teacher stays after school every Thursday to go through problems with her alone. What is the teacher doing?

ctx.s: 考试前，老师每天放学后给我{开小灶}。
ctx.en: Before the exam, the teacher gave me extra one-to-one coaching every day after school.

ctx.s: 这个新人学得慢，师傅专门给他{开了小灶}。
ctx.en: The new apprentice was a slow learner, so the master gave him special extra lessons.

ctx.s: “教练，下课后能不能给我{开个小灶}？我的发球太差了。”
ctx.en: "Coach, could you give me some extra practice after class? My serve is terrible."

ctx.s: 同学们抱怨，班主任总是给成绩好的学生{开小灶}。
ctx.en: The students complain that the form teacher always gives the top students special attention.

ctx.s: 公司给重点项目{开小灶}，资金和人手都优先安排。
ctx.en: The company gives its priority projects special treatment: they get money and staff first.

ctx.s: 同样是新员工，经理凭什么只给他一个人{开小灶}？
ctx.en: We're all new staff, so why does the manager give him alone special one-to-one coaching?

bad.s: 我家厨房太小，所以我们{开小灶}。
bad.en: (meant: our kitchen is small, so we cook on a small stove)
bad.why: It is figurative: extra help or special treatment given to someone, not literally cooking in a small kitchen.

bad.s: 老师上课的时候给全班同学{开小灶}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher taught the whole class in the lesson)
bad.why: It means attention singled out for one person or a few, beyond the normal routine; a regular lesson for the whole class is the opposite.

mean: to make an outrageous demand, such as a sky-high price
lit: the lion opens its mouth wide

use.how: Used as a predicate or after 是、简直是, about someone asking an outrageous price, salary or compensation: 房东狮子大开口，要涨一倍。

near.diff: 冤大头 is the person who ends up paying too much; 狮子大开口 is what the one demanding too much does.

cue: At the airport, a driver sees you are a tourist and asks ten times the normal fare for a short ride into town. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 一碗面要两百块？你这是{狮子大开口}啊！
ctx.en: Two hundred yuan for a bowl of noodles? That's daylight robbery!

ctx.s: 房东{狮子大开口}，房租一下子要涨一倍。
ctx.en: The landlord is making an outrageous demand: he wants to double the rent in one go.

ctx.s: 对方{狮子大开口}，要我们赔一百万，我们当然不能答应。
ctx.en: The other side made an absurd demand for a million in compensation, which of course we can't accept.

ctx.s: 刚毕业就要求月薪五万，是不是有点{狮子大开口}了？
ctx.en: Asking for fifty thousand a month straight out of university: isn't that asking a bit much?

ctx.s: 谈判时，对方一上来就{狮子大开口}，后来才一点点让步。
ctx.en: In the negotiations, they opened with a sky-high demand and only gave ground bit by bit.

ctx.s: 有些景区趁节假日{狮子大开口}，一瓶水卖到二十块。
ctx.en: Some tourist sites take advantage of the holidays to charge absurd prices, twenty yuan for a bottle of water.

bad.s: 他饿坏了，{狮子大开口}，一口吃了半个汉堡。
bad.en: (meant: he was starving and ate half a burger in one big bite)
bad.why: It is about outrageous demands, usually for money, not about eating with a big mouthful.

bad.s: 老板很大方，{狮子大开口}给我们每人发了奖金。
bad.en: (meant: the boss was generous and gave each of us a bonus)
bad.why: It criticises someone who demands far too much; it never describes generous giving.

mean: a sucker who pays far more than they should
lit: a hard-done-by 'big head': the dupe left footing the bill

use.how: A noun, mostly in 当冤大头 or 把…当冤大头: 别把我当冤大头。 Said of someone tricked or pressured into paying too much, often of oneself in rueful self-mockery.

near.diff: 狮子大开口 is what the seller or claimant does in demanding too much; 冤大头 is the person who pays it.

cue: You paid three times the going price for a phone case at a tourist market, then saw the same one for sale round the corner. What were you?

ctx.s: 这件衣服我花了八百，网上才两百，我真是个{冤大头}。
ctx.en: I paid eight hundred for this jacket and it's two hundred online. What a sucker I am.

ctx.s: 他们看你是外地人，把你当{冤大头}了。
ctx.en: They saw you were from out of town and took you for a mug.

ctx.s: 修个水龙头要五百？我可不当这个{冤大头}。
ctx.en: Five hundred to fix a tap? I'm not going to be the sucker who pays that.

ctx.s: 每次聚餐都是他买单，大家早就把他当成{冤大头}了。
ctx.en: He pays every time they eat out; everyone has long since treated him as the one who foots the bill.

ctx.s: 有些商家专门找不懂行情的顾客当{冤大头}。
ctx.en: Some shops specifically target customers who don't know the going rate and overcharge them.

ctx.s: 买房的时候一定要多比较，别做了{冤大头}还不知道。
ctx.en: When buying a flat, compare a lot of offers, or you may end up overpaying without even knowing it.

bad.s: 他头很大，大家都叫他{冤大头}。
bad.en: (meant: he has a big head, so everyone calls him 'big head')
bad.why: It says nothing about the size of anyone's head; it is the person who gets tricked into paying too much.

bad.s: 谢谢你请客，你真是个{冤大头}！
bad.en: (meant: thanks for treating us, you're so generous!)
bad.why: It mocks someone as a gullible sucker; said as thanks for a treat it is an insult, not praise.

r: dǎ zhǒng liǎn chōng pàng zi
mean: to keep up a show beyond one's means just to save face
lit: to slap your own face until it swells, so you look plump and well fed

use.how: Used as a predicate, often in advice with 别、何必: 没钱就别打肿脸充胖子。 Said of spending or promising beyond one's real means to look rich or capable.

near.diff: 爱面子 is caring about face in general; 打肿脸充胖子 is the specific act of pretending to money or ability you lack, at your own cost.

cue: A friend on a modest salary insists on paying for a lavish banquet for ten people, then lives on instant noodles for the rest of the month. What did he do?

ctx.s: 没钱就说没钱，别{打肿脸充胖子}。
ctx.en: If you don't have the money, just say so. Don't pretend you can afford it.

ctx.s: 他工资不高，却非要买名牌包送女朋友，这不是{打肿脸充胖子}吗？
ctx.en: He doesn't earn much, yet he insists on buying his girlfriend a designer bag. Isn't that living beyond his means just for show?

ctx.s: 为了在同学会上有面子，他借钱租了一辆豪车，真是{打肿脸充胖子}。
ctx.en: To look good at the class reunion he borrowed money to rent a luxury car, a show he couldn't really afford.

ctx.s: 这么难的活儿你干不了就直说，何必{打肿脸充胖子}？
ctx.en: If a job this hard is beyond you, just say so. Why pretend you can do it?

ctx.s: 我们公司规模小，展会上没必要{打肿脸充胖子}，租那么大的展位。
ctx.en: We're a small company; there's no need to put on a show at the trade fair by renting such a big stand.

ctx.s: 婚礼办得那么排场，其实是{打肿脸充胖子}，到现在还在还债。
ctx.en: The wedding was so lavish, but it was all for show: they're still paying off the debts.

bad.s: 他最近吃得太多，{打肿脸充胖子}了。
bad.en: (meant: he has been eating too much lately and put on weight)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with gaining weight; it means pretending to be richer or more capable than you are.

bad.s: 他很有钱，所以请大家吃饭就是{打肿脸充胖子}。
bad.en: (meant: being rich, he showed off by treating everyone to dinner)
bad.why: It only applies when someone acts beyond their real means; a rich man treating his friends is not straining to keep up a show.

mean: to suffer a loss one cannot complain about
lit: to swallow a loss in silence, unable to speak of it

use.how: Verb-object phrase, often 吃了个哑巴亏 or 只能吃哑巴亏. Said of a loss you cannot complain about or claim back: no proof, no recourse, or partly your own fault.

near.diff: 背黑锅 is taking the blame for someone else's fault; 吃哑巴亏 is suffering a loss you are in no position to protest.

cue: You paid a deposit in cash with no receipt, and now the landlord denies ever receiving it. There is nothing you can prove or do. What has happened to you?

ctx.s: 没签合同，钱要不回来，只能{吃哑巴亏}了。
ctx.en: There was no contract, so I can't get the money back. I just have to swallow the loss.

ctx.s: 网上买的东西是假的，店铺已经关了，我{吃了个哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: What I bought online was fake and the shop has already closed. I've been cheated with no comeback.

ctx.s: 这件事你一定要留好证据，别到时候{吃哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: Make sure you keep evidence of this, or you'll end up taking a loss you can't do anything about.

ctx.s: 他明知道功劳被同事抢了，可又说不出口，只好{吃了这个哑巴亏}。
ctx.en: He knew his colleague had taken the credit, but he couldn't bring himself to say so and had to swallow it.

ctx.s: “你为什么不去投诉？”“当初是我自己没看清条款，只能{吃这个哑巴亏}。”
ctx.en: "Why don't you complain?" "I didn't read the terms properly myself, so I just have to take the loss."

ctx.s: 小企业被大客户拖欠货款，往往{吃了哑巴亏}也不敢声张。
ctx.en: When big clients pay small firms late, the small firms often suffer in silence and don't dare make a fuss.

bad.s: 他被骗了以后马上报警，还上了新闻，真是{吃了哑巴亏}。
bad.en: (meant: after being cheated he went to the police and was on the news; what a loss)
bad.why: The point is that you cannot speak up or seek redress; someone who went to the police and the press did not suffer in silence.

bad.s: 他{吃哑巴亏}了我。
bad.en: (meant: he made me suffer a loss I couldn't complain about)
bad.why: The subject is the one who suffers, and it takes no object; say ta rang wo chile ge yaba kui (he left me with a loss I couldn't protest).

mean: to switch to a new field late, without formal training
lit: to leave home to become a monk halfway along life's road

story.text: Chujia, 'leaving home', is the Buddhist term for giving up family life to become a monk or nun. Someone who took this step as an adult, after years of ordinary life, rather than entering a temple young, was said to have left home halfway along the road. The phrase was later applied to anyone who takes up a trade or field late, without a grounding in it from the start.
story.source: From the Buddhist term 出家 (to become a monk or nun)

use.how: Used as a predicate or adverbial: 我是半路出家, 半路出家学画画. Said of someone who came to a field late, often modestly about oneself.

near.diff: 门外汉 is an outsider who knows little of the field; 半路出家 is someone now working in it who simply started late, without formal training.

cue: A successful pastry chef explains that she trained as an accountant and only started baking at thirty-five, teaching herself from videos. How does she describe her path?

ctx.s: 我是{半路出家}，以前是学会计的，现在做设计。
ctx.en: I came to this late; I studied accounting and now I work in design.

ctx.s: 他三十多岁才{半路出家}学编程，现在已经是技术骨干了。
ctx.en: He only switched to programming in his thirties, and now he's one of the key engineers.

ctx.s: 别看她是{半路出家}，画得比科班出身的还好。
ctx.en: She may have taken up painting late, but she paints better than people who trained at art school.

ctx.s: “您是专业学音乐的吗？”“不是，我是{半路出家}，自己摸索着学的。”
ctx.en: "Did you study music professionally?" "No, I came to it late and taught myself."

ctx.s: 很多优秀的作家都是{半路出家}，原来的职业五花八门。
ctx.en: Many fine writers came to writing late; their earlier jobs were all kinds of things.

ctx.s: 他知道{半路出家}的人基础不扎实，所以每天都比别人多练两个小时。
ctx.en: He knew that those who switch late lack a solid grounding, so every day he practised two hours more than everyone else.

bad.s: 我们开车去旅游，车坏了，只好{半路出家}。
bad.en: (meant: we were driving on holiday, the car broke down and we had to turn back halfway)
bad.why: It is not about a journey; it means taking up a field or trade late, without formal training.

bad.s: 他从小就学钢琴，后来成了钢琴家，是{半路出家}。
bad.en: (meant: he learned the piano from childhood and became a pianist)
bad.why: It only fits someone who came to the field late; a pianist trained from childhood is the opposite: keban chushen (professionally trained).

mean: to have high standards but little ability to meet them
lit: the eyes are high, the hands are low

use.how: Used as a predicate: 他这个人眼高手低, 有点眼高手低. Criticises someone, often a beginner, who judges or aims high and looks down on modest work but cannot deliver themselves.

near.diff: 好高骛远 is aiming at goals far beyond reach; 眼高手低 stresses the gap between one's judgement and one's actual skill.

cue: A new graduate criticises every report the team writes and turns down simple tasks, but his own first report is full of mistakes. What is his problem?

ctx.s: 他评论别人头头是道，自己一做就错，真是{眼高手低}。
ctx.en: He criticises others very convincingly, but the moment he does it himself he gets it wrong. Great standards, no skill.

ctx.s: 有些刚毕业的学生{眼高手低}，小事不愿做，大事又做不好。
ctx.en: Some new graduates aim too high for their ability: they won't do small jobs and can't do big ones well.

ctx.s: 我学画画的时候也{眼高手低}，看得出好坏，就是画不出来。
ctx.en: When I was learning to paint I had the same problem: I could tell good from bad, I just couldn't paint it.

ctx.s: 面试官最怕招到{眼高手低}的人。
ctx.en: What interviewers fear most is hiring someone whose standards outrun their ability.

ctx.s: “新来的小李怎么样？”“人挺聪明，就是有点{眼高手低}，得让他从基础做起。”
ctx.en: "How's the new guy, Xiao Li?" "Bright enough, but his ambitions outrun his skills. He needs to start from the basics."

ctx.s: 写作要多动笔，光看不练，就容易{眼高手低}。
ctx.en: To write well you have to write a lot; if you only read and never practise, your judgement will outstrip your skill.

bad.s: 他眼光很好，挑的东西都很漂亮，真是{眼高手低}。
bad.en: (meant: he has excellent taste and everything he picks is lovely)
bad.why: It is criticism: high standards with poor ability to meet them, not praise for good taste.

bad.s: 他{眼高手低}了这项工作。
bad.en: (meant: he looked down on this task and did it badly)
bad.why: It describes a person's failing and takes no object; use it of the person: ta zhege ren yan gao shou di.

mean: a hard worker who toils on without complaint
lit: the old yellow ox, the draught animal that ploughs the fields year after year

use.how: A noun: 是…的老黄牛, 像老黄牛一样, also 老黄牛精神. Praises someone, often long-serving, who works hard and steadily without complaint or seeking credit.

near.diff: 挑大梁 is taking the central role; 老黄牛 is the steady, uncomplaining worker, who need not be in charge or in the spotlight.

cue: At a retirement party, a manager praises a clerk who for thirty years came in early, took on every dull job and never once asked for promotion. What was the clerk?

ctx.s: 张师傅是我们厂里的{老黄牛}，三十年没请过一天假。
ctx.en: Master Zhang is our factory's faithful workhorse; he hasn't taken a day off in thirty years.

ctx.s: 我爸一辈子像{老黄牛}一样干活，从来不喊累。
ctx.en: My dad worked like an ox all his life and never once complained of being tired.

ctx.s: 他不爱说话，也不争名利，大家都说他是个{老黄牛}。
ctx.en: He doesn't say much and never chases fame or gain; everyone says he's a real workhorse.

ctx.s: 公司不能只靠几个{老黄牛}撑着，也得给他们涨工资啊。
ctx.en: The company can't just rely on a few uncomplaining hard workers to keep it going; it has to give them a raise too.

ctx.s: “这次评优秀员工，你推荐谁？”“我推荐老刘，他是部门里真正的{老黄牛}。”
ctx.en: "Who do you recommend for employee of the year?" "Lao Liu. He's the one in our department who really keeps quietly working."

ctx.s: 这种埋头苦干、任劳任怨的{老黄牛}精神，值得我们学习。
ctx.en: This spirit of the patient ox, working hard without complaint, is something we should all learn from.

bad.s: 他每天上班都偷懒，真是个{老黄牛}。
bad.en: (meant: he slacks off at work every day, slow as an ox)
bad.why: It praises a hard, uncomplaining worker; for dawdling at work use mo yanggong.

bad.s: 我爷爷已经九十岁了，是个{老黄牛}。
bad.en: (meant: my grandfather is ninety, a very old man)
bad.why: Lao here is part of the image, not a comment on age; it praises tireless work, not being old.
